title: Globally convergent primal-dual active-set methods with inexact subproblem solves
contribution: Three primal-dual active-set methods for structured convex QPs whose reduced linear systems may be solved inexactly at every non-optimal partition: inexactness tests certify subsets of the exact violated sets (via an explicit or dynamically estimated bound on the reduced-Hessian inverse), with finite termination proved under P-/perturbed M-matrix conditions and fewer Krylov iterations on optimal-control QPs.
problem_entry: A cost bottleneck in a fast method: PDAS converges in few iterations but each needs a reduced linear system solve, which at scale is done by Krylov methods; how much inexactness keeps global convergence? Reduction to a BQP rejected because it densifies sparse data (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Identity (7) writes the exact subspace solution as the inexact one plus residual terms, so residual-proportional bounds alpha_I, beta_A certify a nonempty subset of the true violated sets without the exact solve (Lemma 4, pp. 7-8); the needed constant ||R_II^-1|| is either bounded explicitly by an H-matrix procedure (Alg. 2) or replaced by a dynamic gamma raised when KKT progress stalls (Alg. 3); a naive shrinking tolerance (Alg. 4) gets only a weak guarantee (pp. 8-14).
assumptions: Convex QP with equalities and upper bounds on a subset; A_EF invertible and reduced Hessian positive definite (Assumption 1, p. 3); finite termination needs R a P-matrix with extra conditions or R = M + E with M an M-matrix and small ||E|| (Theorem 3, p. 5); exact solves with A_EF (p. 6); inner residuals driven to zero (Theorem 5, p. 8).
proof_devices: finite termination via strictly decreasing potential e^T x_B over finitely many partitions (Theorem 12, p. 20); O(||E||) perturbation for R = M + E (Theorem 13, p. 21)
residual identity (7) with Schur complements and Hoelder bounds (13) to build alpha_I, beta_A (pp. 7, 10)
continuity argument: residual below a partition-dependent epsilon identifies the exact violated sets (Lemma 4 proof, p. 8)
Varga H-matrix bound ||B^-1||_1 <= (min [Bw]_i)^-1 for w in P(B), computed by iteratively solving M(R_II)w ~ e (Lemmas 6-7, pp. 9-10)
contradiction on a growing parameter: if progress stalls forever gamma -> infinity and exceeds max ||R_II^-1|| (Theorem 8, pp. 12-13)
small counterexamples: Example 9 (||R^-1||_1 = 31/4 < 8 = ||R_II^-1||_1, p. 13) and Example 11 (naive tolerance needs exact zero residual, pp. 14-15)
experiments: One Python/cvxopt/MINRES package without preconditioner; exact-solve PDAS and an inexact semismooth Newton (SSN, [30]) reimplemented as rivals; two 2-D elliptic optimal-control QPs on grids 4-64 (n up to 8192), basic and deliberately degenerate instances; PDAS and total Krylov iterations reported (CPU said proportional); inexact variants cut Krylov totals roughly in half vs exact, SSN competitive; parameters 'merely ones that worked well' (pp. 15-19).
positioning: Enhancement of Hintermueller-Ito-Kunisch PDAS [28], whose theorems are generalized (pp. 1, 19); contrasted with slow classical active-set methods (pp. 1-2); gentle comparison with Hintermueller-Stadler inexact SSN [30] (p. 19); builds on own COR@L report [13] (p. 22).
writing: Contribution 'twofold' (p. 2); two anticipated objections answered as 'remarks to make at the outset' (p. 2); each algorithm followed by prose on costs and disadvantages (p. 14); hedged conclusion 'we believe' (p. 19).
limits_future: Limits stated concretely: matrix-structure conditions (p. 5), weak guarantee and hard-to-choose parameters for Alg. 4 (p. 14), no preconditioner (p. 16), untuned parameters (p. 17); only two test problems and no CPU times; no explicit future direction (p. 19).

method_links.note: Inner (Krylov) stopping test derived from what the active-set update must certify (a nonempty subset of the exact violated sets); inexactness allowed at all partitions except optimal ones.
Dynamic gamma raised by a windowed KKT-progress monitor (Alg. 3 step 13): an update rule on observed progress, but controlling inexactness rather than objective vs feasibility.
Intentionally degenerate instances (half zero optimal multipliers, following [4]) reported separately; construction borrowed rather than a new mechanical rule.
Exact baseline differs only in solve accuracy and rival SSN implemented in the same software, same initial partitions; caveat: parameters hand-picked with tuning effort unreported.

transferable: Make the inner stopping test 'the outer step is certified productive' (identify a subset of the true violated indices) using residual bounds from a computable bound on the inverse of the reduced matrix (pp. 7-10).
Replace an expensive problem constant by a monotone dynamic parameter raised only when a windowed progress test fails, and prove it eventually dominates the constant (pp. 12-13).
Certify ||R^-1||_1 by iteratively solving M(R)w ~ e until M(R)w > 0 and applying Varga's bound (pp. 9-10).
Before reformulating for easier theory (QP -> BQP), check whether it destroys sparsity; if so keep the original data (p. 2).
Answer the two obvious referee objections in the introduction as 'remarks at the outset' (p. 2).

quotes.text: a simpler heuristic method that merely decreases a dynamic accuracy tolerance as the optimization process proceeds will not ensure convergence unless one imposes strong requirements on the employed linear system solver
the purpose of our numerical experiments is merely to illustrate the convergence behavior of our algorithms despite inexactness in the subspace solutions

title: Accelerating convergence to competitive equilibrium in electricity markets
contribution: A decentralized market-clearing scheme in which GenCos and DSOs return both their optimal responses and their sensitivities to price, letting the ISO solve an implicit complementarity problem by Fischer-Burmeister semismooth Newton; on IEEE 9-118-bus cases it needs at most 10 iterations and about four orders of magnitude fewer function evaluations than a subgradient method (read from MERL TR2016-095).
problem_entry: Application gap: market research focused on design, little on algorithms; decentralized, privacy-preserving clearing by subgradient price updates is slow and costs many communication rounds (p. 3).
key_idea: Keep the price-signal protocol but have each agent also return dP*/dlambda (analytic for 1-D bound-constrained problems, pp. 6); write the ISO KKT system with best responses substituted as an implicit complementarity problem and solve it by Fischer-Burmeister semismooth Newton with a merit line search (pp. 5-6), following Curtis-Raghunathan [13].
assumptions: Strictly convex GenCo costs, strictly concave DSO utilities (p. 4); DC power flow, single-node DSOs with deferrable loads, price-taking agents who keep costs private (p. 3); strict complementarity of agent problems 'for simplicity' (p. 6); F only piecewise C1 (p. 5).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: competitive equilibrium <-> ICP solution, via KKT conditions of the convex ISO problem (p. 5)
local superlinear convergence cited, not proved (Qi-Sun [18]; PC1 case in [13]) (p. 5)
generalized Jacobian H_k built from diagonal matrices and the agents' sensitivity matrix B_k, following De Luca-Facchinei-Kanzow [20] (p. 6)
experiments: IEEE 9/14/30/39/57/118-bus cases, random utilities and demands, 10 runs averaged, tolerance 1e-6, 100000-iteration cap; untuned 1/(k+1) subgradient baseline hits the cap on 5 of 6 cases while semismooth Newton needs 5-10 iterations, 16-83 function evaluations and 0.01-1.50 s vs 1.42-29.5 s (pp. 6-7).
positioning: Placed in the electricity-equilibrium modelling literature (Hobbs, Baldick, Weber-Overbye, Wang et al.) as filling an algorithmic gap rather than criticizing it; only rival is Shor's subgradient method; method credited to own MERL report [13] (pp. 3, 5).
writing: Short IEEE paper with 'Our Focus'/'Our Contribution' subsections and assumptions (a)-(d) up front (p. 3); headline 'several orders of magnitude speedup' (p. 3) quantified as about 4 orders in function evaluations (p. 7); 'robust' claimed on six cases (p. 7).
limits_future: Stated limits: lumped DSO model, no distributed generation; future: DSO networks with distributed generation, AC power flow, SDP relaxation (p. 7). Not discussed: cost of the extra sensitivity messages, tuned first-order baselines.

method_links.note: The inner solvers (agents) are asked to return exactly what the outer Newton iteration needs (solution sensitivities): inner-serves-outer applied to information content rather than solve accuracy.
10 randomized runs averaged, but the baseline is an untuned 1/(k+1) subgradient method stopped by an iteration cap; no favoured or tuned baseline.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: turn a price-coordination loop into semismooth Newton on the coordinator's complementarity system by asking subproblems for dP*/dlambda

transferable: Write the coordinator's optimality conditions with the agents' best responses substituted as an implicit complementarity problem and apply Fischer-Burmeister semismooth Newton with a merit line search (pp. 5-6).
For one-dimensional bound-constrained agent problems, the solution sensitivity is 1/(second derivative) in the interior and 0 at a bound (p. 6).
Against a first-order coordination baseline, compare oracle calls (agent solves) as well as iterations and time, since communication rounds are the real cost (p. 7).
coauthors: Arvind U. Raghunathan (first author, MERL), Yusuke Takaguchi, Hiroyuki Hashimoto

Still, the number of function evaluations is 4 orders of magnitude smaller than for the subgradient method.

title: A trust region algorithm with a worst-case iteration complexity of for nonconvex optimization
contribution: TRACE, a trust-region method with modified acceptance (decrease relative to ||s||^3), reject-and-expand steps and implicit contractions via quadratic regularization, which matches ARC's O(eps^-3/2) first-order and O(max{eps^-3, eps^-3/2}) second-order worst-case iteration bounds while keeping global convergence and Q-quadratic local convergence with Newton steps.
problem_entry: Gap between traditions: nonconvex methods aimed at global and fast local convergence while worst-case complexity was overlooked; ARC attains O(eps^-3/2) vs O(eps^-2) for traditional trust region; can a trust-region method match ARC and keep its guarantees? (pp. 2-3)
key_idea: Identify ARC's two proof-critical properties of accepted steps (2.4) and redesign the trust-region acceptance (rho_k = decrease/||s||^3) and radius update (reject-and-expand when lambda_k/||s_k|| > sigma_k; contraction by an implicit radius from a regularized subproblem allowing sublinear decrease; cap Delta_k) so that accepted steps satisfy analogues, while allowing unregularized Newton steps (pp. 6-9, 11).
assumptions: f C2; bounded below; Lipschitz gradient and bounded gradients (Assumption 3.1, p. 12); Lipschitz Hessian along the iterate/step path for complexity (Assumption 3.15, p. 20); local: limit point with positive definite Hessian (Assumption 3.29, p. 28); exact Hessians and globally optimal subproblem solutions 'For simplicity', admitted impractical at large scale (pp. 3, 30).
proof_devices: iteration taxonomy A (A_sigma, A_Delta), C, E with at most one expansion between accepted steps (Lemmas 3.7, 3.22, pp. 14-15, 24)
only-contractions implies delta -> 0, lambda -> infinity, then large dual variable forces acceptance (Lemmas 3.8-3.10, pp. 15-16)
bounded sigma_k via ratio bounds after contraction (Lemmas 3.17-3.18, pp. 21-22) and step-norm lower bound ||s_k|| >= (H_Lip + sigma_max)^-1/2 ||g_{k+1}||^1/2 (Lemma 3.19, pp. 22-23)
counting template: #good steps <= (f0 - fmin)/decrease-per-step; contractions between accepted steps bounded by geometric growth of lambda/||s|| to a cap (Lemmas 3.20-3.24, Theorem 3.25, pp. 23-26)
second-order count from lambda_k >= -xi_{k,1} (Lemma 3.27, Theorem 3.28, pp. 27-28)
eventual acceptance of Newton steps gives Q-quadratic rate (Lemma 3.31, Theorem 3.32, pp. 29-30)
eigen-decomposition lower bound on the regularized step norm in contract (Lemma 3.12, pp. 17-18)
experiments: none; the Appendix argues each iteration costs no more than traditional TR or ARC when contract is folded into the secular-equation Newton solve, and that contractions avoid the hard case (pp. 31-32).
positioning: Built directly on ARC (Cartis-Gould-Toint), Nesterov-Polyak and Griewank (pp. 2-3); credits CGT discussions as 'inspirational' (p. 30); distinguishes rather than criticizes ARC (cubic term never 'off', no Newton steps) (pp. 3, 11).
writing: Contribution in the third introduction paragraph (p. 3); a motivation subsection naming the rival's proof inequalities before the algorithm (§2.1, pp. 5-6); three modifications as bullets (p. 7); prose for each unusual step (p. 10); sharpness left explicitly open (p. 30).
limits_future: Exact Hessians and global subproblem solutions; sharpness unconfirmed; no numerical evidence; inexact variants named as 'the subject of current research' (p. 30).

method_links.note: In 2017 the worst-case iteration-complexity yardstick is adopted as the design target and iterations are justified as the measure, without auditing it; the opposite side of his later 'grain of salt' stance.

As in steering, the contribution is a parameter-update rule (radius contraction/expansion, sigma_k) driven by observed step quality, but trading step size against complexity rather than objective against feasibility.

title: A BFGS-SQP Method for Nonsmooth, Nonconvex, Constrained Optimization and its Evaluation using Relative Minimization Profiles
contribution: BFGS-SQP (GRANSO): a penalty-SQP method with BFGS Hessian approximations and Byrd-Nocedal-style penalty steering for nonsmooth, nonconvex constrained problems, without convergence guarantees, evaluated on a new 200-problem controller-design test set with newly introduced relative minimization profiles (RMPs and budget-relative beta-RMPs) that show objective quality, feasibility and cost trade-offs.
problem_entry: Application pull from HIFOO controller design (SFPP fixed-penalty restarts used because gradient sampling is too costly; SQP-GS has guarantees but needs O(n) gradients per iteration) plus an evaluation gap (performance/data profiles need arbitrary binary success criteria) (pp. 3-5).
key_idea: Replace the BFGS direction on the exact penalty by a penalty-SQP QP with BFGS matrix and steer mu by comparing predicted linearized violation reduction with a mu = 0 reference direction (Procedure 1, pp. 6-8); stop via a QP over gradients of recent nearby iterates (pp. 8-9); evaluate with RMPs (fraction of problems whose best feasible objective is within relative difference gamma of the best found) and beta-RMPs at multiples of the new method's per-problem cost (pp. 17-22).
assumptions: f and c continuously differentiable almost everywhere; no convergence claims (pp. 2, 9); test problems spectral radius (non-Lipschitz) and pseudospectral radius (locally Lipschitz) (pp. 11, 14).
proof_devices: n/a for convergence: no theorems; analytic work is definitional design of RMPs (relative differences instead of ratios, p. 19)
equivalence of beta-RMP and RMP for beta >= 1 when budgets come from the method under study (pp. 20-21)
rolling target set (26) maximizing separation per beta (p. 22); measurement-error discussion of the cost axis (pp. 21-22)
experiments: 200 randomly generated controller-design problems (100 spectral, 100 pseudospectral), small sizes to accommodate SQP-GS; rivals SNOPT 7.5 (compiled-code speed advantage stated), SFPP, SQP-GS, BFGS-SQP; tolerances at machine precision and 500 iterations to decouple stopping rules; beta in {1,5,10,inf} relative to BFGS-SQP's per-problem time; spectral set: SQP-GS 78% vs 22% at beta = inf but 26.6x slower, BFGS-SQP 92% at beta = 1; pseudospectral: BFGS-SQP 59% vs 34% and 14.4x faster; regularization ablation over condition caps 10^{2j}; code and test set public (pp. 12-28).
positioning: Continues Lewis-Overton BFGS, own SQP-GS and Byrd-Nocedal(-Waltz/-Lopez-Calva) steering (pp. 3, 6); praises performance profiles ('ingenuity', 'beautiful property') before showing their binary-success deficiency; draws on Moré-Wild data profiles and Birgin et al. (pp. 4-5, 16-20).
writing: Threefold contribution (p. 4); absence of guarantees admitted in the abstract (p. 2); strong results language ('completely outclasses', 'remarkable outcome', p. 26) next to an honest report of SQP-GS wins at beta = inf (pp. 25-26); methodological advice addressed to evaluators (p. 18).
limits_future: No convergence guarantees; small dimensions forced by SQP-GS; single application domain, other problem classes left for future work; regularization effect unexplained and called worth investigating; coarse cost axis (pp. 2, 21-23, 28).

method_links.note: Steering moved into nonsmooth BFGS-SQP; SFPP's fixed schedule leaves the penalty too high for over 100 iterations while BFGS-SQP immediately progresses toward feasibility.
Performance and data profiles audited for their arbitrary binary success criterion; RMPs and beta-RMPs built to show the objective/feasibility/budget trade-off and let the reader define success.

SNOPT's compiled-code advantage stated, extra panels at the faster rivals' budgets, rival's wins printed with numbers, one-component regularization sweep; caveat: c_v, c_mu given without tuning account and infeasible-start check summarized without data.
Hard instances come from a randomized application generator chosen for challenging properties, not mechanical infeasible/degenerate variants of a standard set.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: beta-RMP panels rerun the comparison at budgets equal to multiples of the new method's per-problem cost, so a slower but better rival is judged at equal cost; ranking flips between beta = inf and beta = 1

transferable: Steering for a nonsmooth penalty method: compute the mu = 0 reference direction only when predicted violation reduction is below c_v v(x_k), then shrink mu until the direction achieves a c_v fraction of the reference reduction (p. 8).
Cheap nonsmooth stationarity certificate: minimum-norm element of the penalty-weighted convex hull of gradients at recent nearby iterates, via a QP dual (pp. 8-9).

RMP protocol: tolerances at machine precision, full iterate histories, targets = best feasible values across codes, fraction within relative difference gamma on a log axis including gamma = inf (pp. 18, 22-24).
beta-RMP panel with budgets from the new method's own cost, always beta = 1 and beta = inf, targets re-set per beta; add panels from a faster rival's budgets (pp. 21-22, 26).
Report the rival's best case first with numbers, then the budgets at which the ranking flips (pp. 25-26).

quotes.text: evaluators should aim not to define success but present as much relevant benchmark data as possible in a concise and intuitive manner
the fact remains that SQP-GS actually took 26.6 times longer to run to obtain these better results
